scenarios.title: Duplex mismatch
scenarios.topology: SW1 Gi0/1 <—> PC-A. Cross-over is normal; both run at 100 Mb/s.
scenarios.symptom: File transfers to PC-A crawl. pings succeed but latency spikes. SW1's port error counters climb.

console.out:
Gi0/1 is up, line protocol is up
  Full-duplex, 100Mb/s, media type is RJ45
  input errors 412, CRC 341, late collisions 88

steps.prompt: You see CRC and late-collision counters growing. What do you check next?

choices.label: show interfaces g0/1 (again, look closer)

reveal.out:
Gi0/1 is up, line protocol is up
  Full-duplex, 100Mb/s
  input errors 531, CRC 428, late collisions 121
  Duplex mismatch detected

choices.why: Late collisions + CRC errors on a FastEthernet link are the classic signature of a duplex mismatch.

choices.label: ping 192.168.1.1 (the gateway)
choices.why: Ping succeeds — connectivity is up. It won't explain the poor throughput or the error counters.

choices.label: show version
choices.why: show version reports IOS image and uptime — nothing about the link's duplex state.

steps.prompt: What is the likely root cause?

choices.label: Duplex mismatch (one side full, other half)
choices.why: One end is stuck at half-duplex, the other full-duplex. The half side sees collisions from the full side's simultaneous send, producing late collisions and CRC errors.

choices.label: Bad cable / CRC from interference
choices.why: A bad cable gives high CRC but not a pattern of late collisions tied to duplex.

choices.label: Wrong subnet mask
choices.why: Wrong mask would break reachability, not cause late collisions.

scenarios.resolution: Set both ends the same: either both auto-negotiate, or force full-duplex/100 on both the switch port and the NIC. After the fix, error counters stop incrementing.

scenarios.title: Wrong subnet mask
scenarios.topology: PC-A (192.168.1.10) and PC-B (192.168.1.20) on the same switch VLAN; router .1 is the gateway.
scenarios.symptom: PC-A can ping its own address and the router but cannot ping PC-B, even though they are on the same /24.

steps.prompt: PC-A can't reach PC-B. What's the next diagnostic?

choices.label: ipconfig /all on PC-A
choices.why: The mask 255.255.0.0 (/16) makes PC-A treat the whole 192.168.0.0/16 as local — so it never sends to the gateway for 192.168.1.20, and PC-B (correctly /24) does the same the other way.

choices.label: ping 8.8.8.8
choices.why: That tests Internet path, not the same-LAN reachability that's failing.

choices.label: arp -a
choices.why: ARP shows only entries the host already resolved — it won't show why PC-A skips the gateway.

choices.label: Wrong subnet mask on PC-A
choices.why: Hosts must agree on the mask to decide whether a destination is local or remote. The /16 breaks that decision for both.

choices.label: Wrong default gateway
choices.why: The gateway address is correct; the mask is what's corrupting the local/remote decision.

choices.label: PC-B is powered off
choices.why: Then PC-A's ARP would get no reply at all — but the mask is already visible as wrong on PC-A.

scenarios.resolution: Change PC-A's mask to 255.255.255.0 (/24). Both hosts now agree 192.168.1.20 is local and PC-A can ARP it.

scenarios.title: Missing default gateway
scenarios.topology: PC-A (192.168.1.10/24) on VLAN 10; router R1 (.1) provides the gateway to the Internet.
scenarios.symptom: PC-A can reach PC-B on the same LAN and the router, but cannot reach anything off-subnet (e.g., 8.8.8.8).

steps.prompt: Same-LAN works, off-subnet fails. What do you inspect?

choices.label: ipconfig /all (check default gateway)
choices.why: A gateway of 0.0.0.0 (or blank) means the host has no route off-subnet — it can't even attempt the hop to R1 for remote destinations.

choices.label: arp -a
choices.why: ARP only matters for local delivery; there's nothing wrong with local delivery here.

choices.label: ping 8.8.8.8
choices.why: You already know it fails; it doesn't tell you why.

choices.label: No default gateway configured on PC-A
choices.why: Without a default gateway, the host discards off-subnet traffic — there is no next hop to send it to.

choices.label: R1 is down
choices.why: But PC-A can ping 192.168.1.1, so R1 (and the link) is up.

choices.label: DNS is broken
choices.why: DNS would explain name resolution failures, not a bare-IP failure to 8.8.8.8.

scenarios.resolution: Configure PC-A's default gateway as 192.168.1.1. Off-subnet traffic now routes through R1.

scenarios.title: DNS failure
scenarios.topology: PC-A (192.168.1.10/24, gateway 192.168.1.1). Internet reachable by IP.
scenarios.symptom: PC-A can ping 8.8.8.8 (pure IP) but `ping www.cisco.com` fails with 'unable to resolve'. The browser shows DNS errors.

steps.prompt: IP works, names don't. What's the next test?

choices.label: nslookup www.cisco.com

reveal.out:
Server:  UnKnown
Address:  192.168.1.1

*** UnKnown can't find www.cisco.com: Non-existent domain

choices.why: nslookup isolates DNS specifically. A timeout / non-existent-domain reply points straight at DNS configuration, not routing.

choices.label: ping 192.168.1.1
choices.why: Gateway ping already succeeds; it won't reveal anything about name resolution.

choices.label: traceroute 8.8.8.8
choices.why: Traceroute verifies the path to the IP, which already works.

choices.label: DNS server misconfigured / unreachable
choices.why: With a working IP path but failing resolution, the DNS server setting (or the server itself) is the problem — the resolver is pointed at something that can't answer.

choices.label: Default gateway wrong
choices.why: The gateway is fine — 8.8.8.8 pings through it.

choices.label: The site is down
choices.why: The error is a resolution failure (name ≠ address), not a connection refusal — the site being down would give a different error.

scenarios.resolution: Point PC-A's DNS to a working server (e.g., 8.8.8.8) or fix the internal DNS forwarder. Name resolution starts working while IP paths stay unchanged.
